newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba closes youth festival with dance, music.
newsitem.headline: Cuba closes youth festival with dance, music.

text.p: With President Fidel Castro presiding, Cuba closed a nine-day leftist international youth festival on Tuesday with a slick pageant of dance, music and fireworks.
Castro waved to the crowd of some 12,335 delegates from 132 countries at Havana's Panamerican stadium.

But despite several chanted pleas of "Fidel, Fidel" from the crowd urging him to speak, Castro did not address the gathering. The Cuban leader, who turns 71 in one week, has not made a public speech since April.

But Castro, well known for his speech-making, has periodically lapsed into public silence in the past. And while there have been no speeches recently, Cuban state television showed him at the weekend in a relaxed mood meeting delegates to the festival.

Tuesday's ceremony closed an event that has revived a tradition of periodic leftist youth gatherings that had faltered since the last such meeting in Pyongyang, North Korea in 1989 -- before the demise of communism in the former Soviet Union and eastern Europe.

The event, for "anti-imperialist solidarity, peace and friendship", gathered enthusiastic leftist youths and students to a series of political debates and concerts and focused heavily on condemnations of U.S. "imperialism" and the woes of capitalism.

Cuba, isolated since it lost its old economic and political partner the Soviet Union, clearly sought to use the event to show it has friends around the world. Hosting such a gathering also reflected a certain official confidence that the island has come through the worst of economic crisis that hit a low in 1993-94.

Tuesday's ceremony began with the reading of a closing festival declaration that included a long wish list for change in the world. The declaration denounced NATO, nuclear arms, racism and xenophobia, discrimination against women, foreign military bases and development policies that ignore the environment, and demanded the cancellation of developing countries' foreign debt.

It called for respect for human rights by governments but also declared that every country should have the right to choose its own system of democracy. And drawing a loud cheer from the crowd, it denounced the 35-year-old U.S. economic embargo against Cuba.

The ceremony moved on to a pageant depicting the cultures of the different continents, with a sea of extragantly-costumed dancers ranging through images of African tribes and karate to ballet and blues. Cuban state media said some 7,000 dancers, young people and children took part in the show.
A large "human blackboard" -- children who had spent months practising with their cards -- along one side of the stadium threw up a backdrop of changing images.

The festival was dedicated to Argentine-born leftist guerrilla Ernesto "Che" Guevara, killed 30 years ago this year. At the end of the ceremony the human blackboard depicted the famous Korda photograph of a pensive Guevara, while a diminutive schoolboy with a neat tie and polished hair sang a well-known ballad to the revolutionary.

The overtones of an Olympic Games ceremony -- without the commercial billboards lining the stadium -- were completed when a flame shot out dramatically from a large urn suspended over the portrait of Guevara.
